51.quote_or_event: “If in time of distress, when the meal of the whole family is cooked by the water of a small pot, if a host of relatives sufficient to consume the water of the sea should come all at once, the softly-speaking woman, who shows herself as bounteous as the ocean, is the glory of her house.”
51.explanation: The Jain-authored Tamil Nālaṭiyār praises the wife who stretches scant household means into generous hospitality without complaint.
51.tie_back: Valluvar's ideal partner has the household virtues and orders the home to suit her husband's means, and this quatrain shows exactly that: hospitality matched to a meagre pot.
51.source: Nālaṭiyār ch. 39 'Chaste Women', st. 2 (= st. 382), English translation in The Indian Antiquary
51._accuracy_note: A Tamil Jain text, used because no canonical scripture addresses a wife's household management this closely. Quoted from the Indian Antiquary translation on wisdomlib, not Pope's.

52.quote_or_event: “This Revai, the wife of that Mahasayaga, possessed ancestral property consisting of eight kror measures of gold and eight herds, each herd containing ten thousand head of cattle.” Yet in the canon's story Revati, ruled by greed and craving, does away with her co-wives, takes to meat and drink, and tries to pull her husband, a lay disciple of Mahavira, out of his vowed retreat, while he silently 'continued in the meditation of the Law'.
52.explanation: The seventh Anga sets a household of enormous wealth and a devout husband beside a wife without virtue. Revati's own riches cannot save her: she dies within seven days and, the text says, is reborn in hell.
52.tie_back: Valluvar says that if a wife lacks the excellence of domestic virtue, whatever greatness a household has is nothing, and Mahasataka's house, though one of the richest in Rajagriha, is undone by Revati's conduct.
52.source: Uvāsagadasāo, Lecture 8 (Mahāsayaga), §§ 233–257, esp. § 234 and § 247 (tr. A. F. Rudolf Hoernle, Bibliotheca Indica, vol. 2, Calcutta, 1888; scan at archive.org)
52._accuracy_note: § 234 and the phrase from § 247 checked against the archive.org OCR of Hoernle's translation, with obvious OCR slips corrected ('thonsand', 'Mahisayaga'), and the narrative summary follows §§ 238–257. It is a negative example, a bad wife in a rich house, not a positive teaching on a wife's virtue, so the fit with the Kural is strong but indirect.

53.quote_or_event: “Though her house be open on the four quarters, though it be exceedingly small, and though the rain pour in on every side, a chaste and virtuous woman will be honoured in the place where she resides, and her habitation respected.”
53.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār says a virtuous wife makes even a poor, leaking hut a place of honour.
53.tie_back: This is the positive half of Valluvar's paired question: when the wife is excellent nothing is lacking, even in a house with nothing in it.
53.source: Nālaṭiyār ch. 39 'Chaste Women', st. 3 (= st. 383), English translation in The Indian Antiquary
53._accuracy_note: A Tamil Jain text close in idiom to the Kural. It gives only the positive half of the couplet, and the translation is the Indian Antiquary one on wisdomlib.

54.quote_or_event: In Vimalasūri's Paumacariya, the earliest Jain Rāmāyaṇa, Sītā enters the fire-ordeal to prove her chastity and the blazing pit turns into a lake of water, after which she renounces the world and becomes a Jain nun.
54.explanation: The Jain telling makes Sītā's steadfast fidelity a force strong enough to quench fire, and then has her turn that same firmness to renunciation.
54.tie_back: Valluvar asks what treasure is greater than a woman whose karpu has inner firmness, and the Jain Sītā is a firmness that even fire cannot overcome.
54.source: Vimalasūri, Paumacariya (Prakrit, c. 4th century CE), the fire-ordeal episode; summarised in 'Paumacariya (critical study)', wisdomlib.org
54._accuracy_note: The ordeal-turned-lake is confirmed from secondary summaries; I did not consult a primary translation. The miracle also appears in Hindu tellings, but the turn to Jain renunciation is distinctively Jain.

55.quote_or_event: When the gates of Campā could not be opened, a voice from the sky said they would open only if a true woman (satī) drew water from the well with a sieve on a weak cotton thread and sprinkled it on them; the slandered laywoman Subhadrā did this and the gates opened.
55.explanation: The tale of Subhadrā, one of the Jain sixteen satīs, makes a wife's proven chastity a power that commands water and stone where everyone else fails.
55.tie_back: Valluvar's chaste wife says 'rain' and it rains, and Subhadrā holds water in a sieve and opens sealed gates: the same belief that a chaste wife can command the natural order.
55.source: Āvaśyaka-cūrṇi of Jinadāsa (story of Subhadrā); summarised in Jainpedia, 'Subhadrā'
55._accuracy_note: Confirmed from Jainpedia. Subhadrā's power comes from chastity and Jain faith, not from treating her husband as a god, so the theology of 'worshipping no god but her husband' does not carry over.

56.quote_or_event: Añjanāsundarī, rejected by her husband Pavanañjaya on their wedding night, stayed faithful in her in-laws' house and loved him from a distance; later she was banished by her in-laws on a false charge of unchastity and gave birth to Hanumān in a forest cave, until her fidelity was vindicated.
56.explanation: In the Jain Rāma tradition Añjanā is the satī who protects her own virtue and her husband's name through long neglect and false accusation without ever giving way.
56.tie_back: Valluvar defines the wife as one who guards herself, cherishes her husband, keeps the household's name unstained and never slackens, and Añjanā's story is a lifetime of exactly that steadiness under the worst conditions.
56.source: Jain Rāma narratives (Paumacariya; Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭi-śalākā-puruṣa-caritra, Book VII); summarised in Jainpedia, 'Añjanāsundarī'
56._accuracy_note: Confirmed from Jainpedia. Traditional details such as the length of the separation vary between versions and are left out, and the story stresses endurance more than active care of the household.

57.quote_or_event: “When Râgîmatî perceived that Rathanêmi's strength of will was broken, and temptation had got the better of him, she did not lose her presence of mind and defended her Self on that occasion. The daughter of the best king, true to self-control and her vows, maintained the honour of her clan and family, and her virtue …”
57.explanation: Alone in a cave with no one to protect her, Rājīmatī guards herself purely by inner resolve and recalls her tempter to his vows.
57.tie_back: Valluvar says walls and watchmen accomplish nothing and that the only real guard is a woman's own inner steadiness, which is exactly how Rājīmatī, with no outside protection, defends herself.
57._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com. Rājīmatī is a nun and Ariṣṭanemi's abandoned bride, not a wife in a household, but the self-guarding principle is a near-exact match.

58.quote_or_event: “The observance of the five minor vows of the layman, without committing transgressions thereof, bears fruit in the shape of a birth in the heaven-worlds where [the soul] acquires clairvoyance (avadhi jnana), the eight kinds of miraculous powers and a divine body. The low caste Tampala [in respect of the first], Dhanadeva [in respect of the second], then Varisena, Nili and Jayakumar [in respect of the third, fourth and fifth vows respectively] have risen to high, worshipful status.”
58.explanation: Samantabhadra promises heavenly birth to lay votaries who keep the minor vows, and names the laywoman Nīlī as the exemplar of the chastity vow who rose to honoured status.
58.tie_back: Valluvar promises great glory in the gods' world to women who keep faith with their husbands, and the Jain text gives the faithful laywoman Nīlī, along with every vow-keeper, heavenly birth and honour.
58.source: Samantabhadra, Ratnakaraṇḍa Śrāvakācāra vv. 63–64, tr. Champat Rai Jain, 1917, pp. 30–31
58._accuracy_note: Verified against the archive.org OCR (spelling slightly normalised from the OCR). Verse numbers follow the standard Sanskrit numbering because Champat Rai's edition is unnumbered. The reward comes from keeping a vow, not from honouring a husband, so the fit is partial.

59.quote_or_event: In Vimalasūri's Paumacariya, Rāma sends the pregnant Sītā into exile because of public scandal about her, though she is innocent; she gives birth to Lavaṇa and Aṅkuśa in the forest and is later vindicated before the people.
59.explanation: The Jain Rāmāyaṇa shows a king who believed his public standing depended on his wife's reputation, while making clear that the slander, not Sītā, was at fault.
59.tie_back: Valluvar says a man whose wife does not guard the household's name cannot walk proudly before his detractors; the Jain epic shows the same tie between a wife's name and a husband's public standing, though from the side of an unjustly slandered wife.
59.source: Vimalasūri, Paumacariya, the exile-of-Sītā episode; summarised in 'Paumacariya (critical study)', wisdomlib.org
59._accuracy_note: Next-best match. The underlying assumption is shared, but here the wife is blameless, which reverses the Kural's case. Confirmed only from secondary summaries.

60.quote_or_event: “From the moment that this our boy has been begotten, our silver increased, our gold increased, &c. … Therefore when this our boy will be born, we shall give him the fit name, attributive and conformable to his quality--Vardhamāna.”
60.explanation: Siddhārtha and Triśalā name their son Vardhamāna, 'the increasing one', because the household's wealth, glory and liberality grew from the moment he was conceived.
60.tie_back: Valluvar calls the wife's excellence the home's blessing and good children its jewel, and the Kalpa Sūtra presents Triśalā's household as one whose good fortune is crowned by the birth of a child.
60.source: Kalpa Sūtra, Life of Mahāvīra §91 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
60._accuracy_note: Verified on wisdomlib's Jacobi text. A strong image of a child as the household's ornament, but the passage praises the child's merit, not the wife's virtue, so it covers only half of the couplet.
